title: Methodology
text: Plain-language explainer. For the formal model, identification assumptions, and full robustness battery, see the working paper PDF.

title: Methodology
text:
Why this matters
Cross-border payments depend on banks talking to other banks through a network called correspondent banking. Over the last decade, banks have been quietly walking away from each other — closing accounts, dropping relationships, refusing to clear payments through certain country pairs. Regulators call this de-risking.
Not all trade is hit equally. Simple commodities can be paid for with cash, prepayment, or a single bank transfer. Complex products — semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, machinery — are different. They typically need a chain of trust: letters of credit, several banks acting in sequence, foreign-exchange settlement, extended payment terms. When the chain breaks, the kinds of trade that depend most on the chain are the kinds that get cut first.
Stablecoins — dollar-denominated digital tokens that move on blockchain networks — bypass the bank-to-bank chain entirely. The question is simple: where would they help most?

title: Methodology
text:
The intuition
If payment-network problems hit complex trade harder than simple trade, the data should show a clean signature. We use three real-world events that pushed payment frictions in opposite directions:

FATF greylisting (friction up). The global anti-money-laundering body publishes a watch list. Once listed, banks abroad become more cautious about clearing the country’s payments.
EU AMLD harmonization (friction down). EU members adopted common AML rules in 2017. Within EU corridors, banks became more confident, not less.
FDI-derisked corridors (friction up). When bilateral foreign-direct-investment positions collapse, the underlying financial relationship has typically broken. We mark a corridor de-risked if FDI fell more than 50% from its 2015–2017 average.

A spurious channel — a generic “advanced economies do better” story — cannot produce opposite signs on opposite-direction shocks. The fact that AMLD pulls one way while FATF and FDI pull the other way is the cleanest causal-mechanism evidence available in this setting.

title: Methodology
Methodology
text:
What this is good for
The estimated effects aggregate into a country-level Stablecoin Opportunity Score — a ranking of where alternative payment infrastructure would unlock the most economically valuable trade.

The composite top five are Haiti, Fiji, Syria, Lebanon, and Nicaragua — small economies with high friction exposure and limited regulatory alternatives.
A second filter looks at where stablecoins could plausibly deploy today (capital-account openness × infrastructure readiness); within those 60 “actionable now” jurisdictions the top ten by SOS are Panama, Trinidad and Tobago, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Georgia, San Marino, Uruguay, Oman, Armenia, and Kuwait.

title: Methodology
section: What this analysis is — and isn’t
text:
What this analysis is — and isn’t
This is a preliminary analysis using publicly available data. Three limitations follow:

Direct correspondent-banking data, ideally from BIS or SWIFT, would sharpen the test. Our FDI-based de-risking measure is a coarse stand-in for actual bank-to-bank account closures.
Higher computing power would let us run the full panel rather than subsamples on the heaviest specifications. The full bilateral panel has roughly 33 million observations and does not fit in 16 GB of memory under the four-fixed-effect Poisson estimator we use for robustness; we use a stratified 3,000-pair subsample for those specifications.
The Chainalysis Global Crypto Adoption Index would replace the GDP-per-capita placeholder we use as the second axis of the feasibility filter — a behavioral measure of where stablecoin infrastructure already exists, rather than a developmental proxy.

What this analysis can show with public data is the direction and order of magnitude of where stablecoins would help most and where they would help least. It cannot say exactly which corridors will respond first, or how fast adoption would translate into trade. Those questions need private data and longer time series.
Read the full working paper (PDF)

title: Data
text:
Limitations and disclosure
This is a preliminary analysis using publicly available data. Three caveats:

The de-risking measure is a proxy. We do not observe correspondent-banking account closures directly; we use bilateral FDI collapses as a stand-in. Direct CBR data from the BIS Statistics on Correspondent Banking or SWIFT would sharpen the test.
Heaviest specifications run on a subsample. The full bilateral × product × year panel exceeds the memory available under a four-fixed-effect Poisson estimator. A 3,000-pair stratified subsample is used for the most demanding specifications; the main results are robust to this restriction (see the paper’s robustness section).
Infrastructure axis is a placeholder. GDP per capita / internet penetration is a coarse stand-in for where stablecoin infrastructure actually exists. The Chainalysis Global Crypto Adoption Index would be a direct replacement.

title: About
text:
The Stablecoin Opportunity Map asks where alternative payment infrastructure — specifically dollar-denominated stablecoins on public blockchain rails — would unlock the most economically valuable trade.
The premise is that complex products (semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, machinery) depend on a fragile bank-to-bank chain of trust to clear payment, and that this chain has been quietly breaking under post-2014 de-risking pressure. If stablecoins bypass the chain, the marginal value of adoption should be highest where the chain is most strained and the underlying trade is most complex. This site lets you see the framework applied country-by-country.

title: The Stablecoin Opportunity Map
text:
How to read this

Composite SOS rolls up three independent natural experiments — FATF greylisting, FDI-derisked corridors, and EU AMLD harmonization — into a single country-level score. Higher = more exposure to correspondent-banking frictions on complex-goods trade.
Three components (FATF / FDI / AMLD) decompose the headline score and identify which channel dominates for each country.
Quadrants combine the SOS with two readiness dimensions (capital openness × infrastructure) so an analyst can separate high-need from actionable-now jurisdictions.
